title: Hinduism: dharma
hookLine: Hindus speak of dharma, the right order of things and the right way for each life

cards: Some mornings are clear about what they're for. The kid needs breakfast, the shift starts at eight, the friend in the hospital needs a visit.
Other mornings arrive with ten possible lives on a phone screen, the travel one, the start-up one, the monk one, each shinier than the one at hand.
Hindus have a word that holds both of those mornings: the big order of the universe, and the small right way for this one life, today. Some Hindus call their whole tradition by it: dharma.

teach.b: Sanskrit grammarians trace dharma to a root, dhri, meaning to hold, to support, to keep something standing. Dharma is what holds things up.
In the widest sense it's the order of the cosmos: the sun rising, the seasons turning, the world held together rather than falling apart.
In society it's what holds people together: justice, truthfulness, duty to family, care for guests and the poor.
And in a single life it's the particular right way for you, at your stage of life, in your place. A student's dharma is to learn. A parent's is to raise children.
A king's, in the old stories, is to protect.
Some Hindus call their tradition Sanatana Dharma, the eternal dharma, and explain that it's less a set of beliefs than the way things truly hold together.
In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells the warrior Arjuna it's better to do your own dharma, even imperfectly, than someone else's dharma well.
Svadharma, your own dharma. Not the neighbor's path, however shiny. How far a person's dharma is set by birth is an old argument among Hindus, and some Hindus today firmly reject tying it to caste.
Other Indian traditions, Buddhist, Jain and Sikh, use the word dharma too, each in its own sense. This week, we're guests at a Hindu table.
And on a plain weekday, the question dharma asks is simple: what holds things up, here, today, and what is mine to hold?

how: Hindus often speak of daily life in terms of dharma: duties to family, work, community and the gods, suited to one's stage of life, and some call their tradition Sanatana Dharma.

o: what holds things up: the world's order, and each life's right way
the good or bad that comes back to you from your past deeds
a fixed fate that's been written for you since before birth

s: it means what holds things up: the cosmic order, social duty, and the right way for each life.
the Gita says your own dharma, done imperfectly, is better than another's done well
all Hindus agree on how dharma relates to birth

games.q: you're good at your own work, but a friend's career looks more exciting. what does the Gita's line suggest?
o: switch to theirs; do it well.
do your own dharma, even imperfectly.
games.why: Krishna tells Arjuna that one's own dharma, even imperfectly done, is better than another's done well.

practice: Think about the roles you hold right now, child, parent, friend, worker, neighbor, student, and let one rise that needs you today. In that role, what's the one thing that would help hold things up?
Not a whole life plan, just today's piece: name it plainly inside.

wordCard.voice: Dharma. From the Sanskrit for to hold: the order that holds the world up, and the right way for each life within it. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: what holds up; order, duty, the right way.

carryVoice: Your line: my own dharma. Yours to hold, even imperfectly. That's day two hundred thirty-three.
